questions.prompt: How does error handling work in Go, and why doesn't Go use exceptions?
options: Wrapping an error with %w discards the original, so errors.Is can no longer match it.
Errors are ordinary return values checked at each call site, wrapped with %w and inspected with errors.Is/As; panic is reserved for unrecoverable bugs.
Errors propagate up the stack automatically until a top-level handler catches them.

Go has try/catch under the names defer and recover, and idiomatic code panics on any expected failure such as a missing record or a closed file, which is why the standard library never returns error values.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you've internalized Go's philosophy or are translating exception habits into Go syntax.

Model answer: Go treats errors as ordinary return values, not a separate control-flow channel. A function that can fail returns (result, error), and the caller checks err != nil immediately rather than letting failures propagate implicitly. This makes failure paths visible in the code, at the cost of verbosity. Errors can be wrapped with fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err) to add context while preserving the original for errors.Is and errors.As.

.NET parallel: The sharpest philosophical difference from C#. In .NET, exceptions are the default for anything unexpected and can bubble to global middleware. Go treats all failure as values, even expected ones like "not found", so every call site needs an explicit decision. panic/recover exists, but idiomatic Go reserves it for truly unrecoverable programmer errors; using panic like a C# exception is a tell of someone still thinking in .NET.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between a pointer receiver and a value receiver on a Go method?
options: Mixing both receiver kinds on one type is the recommended idiom for clarity.
A value receiver works on a copy, so mutations are lost; a pointer receiver works on the original. If any method needs a pointer, use pointers for all.

They behave identically, because Go passes every struct by reference automatically, just like a class instance in C#, and a pointer receiver is only needed when the method is called from another package.
Pointer receivers copy the struct, while value receivers mutate the original.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you understand Go's value semantics well enough to avoid subtle mutation and copying bugs.

Model answer: A method with a value receiver (func (s Subscriber) Name() string) operates on a copy; mutating fields doesn't affect the original. A pointer receiver (func (s *Subscriber) SetName(n string)) operates on the original. Rule of thumb: if any method needs a pointer receiver (to mutate, or because the struct is large), make all methods on that type use pointer receivers.

.NET parallel: Loosely like C# struct versus class. The twist: in Go everything defaults to value semantics unless you use a pointer, whereas in C# anything declared class is a reference. A C# developer's instinct is to assume Go structs behave like classes, and they don't unless you hold a pointer.

questions.prompt: How does Go's interface system differ from interfaces in C# or Java?
options: Types from third-party packages can never satisfy an interface you define later.
Go interfaces can only contain fields, never methods.
A Go type must declare implements on every interface it satisfies, which is why large interface hierarchies are designed up front before any type exists.
Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly by matching method sets, so small interfaces are defined at the point of use: accept interfaces, return structs.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Understanding of structural typing, which changes how you'd design the adapter contract.

Model answer: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly: a type has the right method signatures and the compiler matches it, with no implements keyword. You can define an interface after a type exists, describing only the behaviour a call site needs, and any type, even from a third-party library, satisfies it if the shapes line up.

.NET parallel: C# interfaces are nominal (class Adapter : IPartnerAdapter). In Go it's idiomatic to define small, narrow interfaces where they're used. For the Integration Hub, a new partner adapter just needs a Send(Event) error method to satisfy the platform's interface; it doesn't register anything.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between make([]T, 0) and var s []T, and when does it matter?
options: var s []T is a nil slice and make([]T, 0) is an empty non-nil one; most operations treat them alike, but nil marshals to JSON null and empty to [].
They are identical in every way, including how encoding/json serializes them.
A nil slice panics on len and range, so it must always be checked first.

make([]T, 0) allocates a large default capacity, while var s []T can't be appended to until it has been initialized with make, which is why idiomatic Go code always prefers make over var for every slice.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Attention to Go's nil-versus-empty slice distinction, a classic quick-fire question.

Model answer: var s []T creates a nil slice (len 0, cap 0, s == nil); make([]T, 0) creates a non-nil empty slice. len, append and range behave the same on both. It matters for JSON: a nil slice marshals to null, an empty slice to []. If an API promises an array is never null, initialize with make or check before marshaling.

.NET parallel: Directly analogous to a null List<T> versus new List<T>(), with the same JSON gotcha: System.Text.Json also serializes a null collection as null.

questions.prompt: What does defer do, and what's the common mistake with defer inside a loop?
options: defer runs its call at the end of each loop iteration, so deferring Close() inside a loop releases every file as soon as that iteration finishes, and nothing piles up even in very long-running loops.
defer runs the call immediately but asynchronously on a new goroutine.
Deferred calls are skipped when the function returns an error or panics.
defer runs a call when the enclosing function returns; deferring in a long loop delays every cleanup until the function ends, so resources pile up.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Practical Go hygiene: resource cleanup and a classic footgun.

Model answer: defer schedules a call to run when the enclosing function returns, however it returns, and is used for cleanup right next to where a resource is opened. The mistake: deferring inside a loop with many iterations. None of the deferred calls run until the whole function returns, so resources stay open far longer than intended. Fix: extract the loop body into its own function so defer scopes to each iteration.

.NET parallel: Comparable to C#'s using, but inverted: a using inside a for loop disposes per iteration (block-scoped), while Go's defer in a loop waits for function end. Explaining that contrast shows real command of both languages.

questions.prompt: How would you structure a Go project with multiple packages, and what goes in internal/?
options: cmd/ holds entry points and internal/ holds code only this module may import (compiler-enforced); the adapter contract other teams use stays exported.
internal/ is only a naming convention, and the compiler does not enforce anything.
Go projects must keep all code in a single package called main.
Put everything, including the adapter contract that partner teams must implement against, under internal/ so that external code can depend on it safely.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Familiarity with Go project layout, relevant for a platform other teams integrate with.

Model answer: A typical layout separates cmd/ (entry points), internal/ (importable only from within the module, enforced by the compiler) and sometimes pkg/ (shared code; a debated convention). For the Integration Hub, the adapter contract other teams implement should live in an exported package, while routing and storage internals sit under internal/ so others can't depend on details that might change.

.NET parallel: internal/ is like C#'s internal access modifier, restricting a type to its assembly; Go enforces it per directory tree within a module. Marking shared-library types internal versus public to control what other teams reference is the same instinct.

questions.prompt: What happens if you send on a closed channel, and what about receiving from one?
options: Receivers should close a channel once they've read enough values.
Sending on a closed channel blocks until it's reopened, and receiving from one blocks forever, so a receiver can never tell a channel was closed.
Sending on a closed channel panics; receiving returns the zero value immediately, and v, ok := <-ch reports ok == false. Only the sender closes.
Both operations silently do nothing and return without any error.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Precise channel semantics, a common quick technical check.

Model answer: Sending on a closed channel panics. Receiving from a closed channel never blocks: it returns the zero value, and the two-value form (v, ok := <-ch) returns ok == false to distinguish closed from a real zero value. Convention: only the sender closes, to signal no more values; closing from the receiver or closing twice panics.

.NET parallel: The closest analog is a completed Channel<T> from System.Threading.Channels: reading after completion returns immediately and writing throws. BlockingCollection<T>.CompleteAdding() is an older, rougher parallel.

questions.prompt: How does Go's garbage collector affect how you write a high-throughput service?
options: Allocate more pointers, because heap allocations are cheaper than values.
The GC is concurrent and low-pause, but allocation churn still costs CPU; profile with pprof, reuse buffers with sync.Pool, and avoid needless heap allocs.
Disable the GC in production, since its pauses are always seconds long.
It doesn't matter at all: Go has no garbage collector, because every value lives on the stack and is freed when its function returns, which also makes pprof and sync.Pool pointless.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you think about performance beyond "write correct code and hope."

Model answer: Go's GC is concurrent and generally low-pause, so it rarely needs tuning, but heavy allocation churn still adds GC pressure and CPU overhead. Mitigations: reuse buffers via sync.Pool, prefer values over pointers where a heap allocation isn't needed, and profile with pprof before optimizing. For an integration platform this matters most in the hot path: validation and serialization.

.NET parallel: Comparable to .NET's generational GC with the same advice: avoid allocations in hot paths, use ArrayPool<T> or pooling, and profile (dotnet-trace) instead of guessing. Only the tool names change.

questions.prompt: How would you fetch data from five APIs concurrently in Go and combine the results?
options: Start a goroutine per call writing to a channel or an indexed slice, wait with sync.WaitGroup, then close the channel; decide upfront how partial failures behave.
Start the goroutines and read the results immediately without waiting for them to finish.
Use a global variable that every goroutine appends to without any synchronization.
Call the five APIs one after another inside a single goroutine, because Go's scheduler parallelizes sequential HTTP calls on its own behind the scenes, merging the responses once they all arrive.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Practical fluency with goroutines, channels and sync.WaitGroup; likely live-coding.

Model answer: Launch a goroutine per API call, each writing its result to a shared channel (or a pre-sized slice by index, which avoids a mutex). Use sync.WaitGroup to know when all have finished, then close the channel so a range over it terminates. Handle partial failure explicitly: does one failed call fail everything or just get omitted?

.NET parallel: Directly analogous to Task.WhenAll over a list of Task<T>. Goroutines are lighter-weight and have no async state machine; channels are the explicit way to get results back instead of an awaited return value.

questions.prompt: What is a race condition, and how would you detect one in Go?
options: A race condition is any slow goroutine, and you detect it by timing each function call and flagging whichever one finishes last in the benchmark.
Concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write and no synchronization; Go's built-in race detector (go test -race) reports the exact accesses.
Go prevents races at compile time, so no runtime tooling is needed.
Races only happen in programs that use more than one CPU core.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Awareness of Go's built-in tooling, not just the concept.

Model answer: A race occurs when two goroutines access the same memory concurrently, at least one writes, and there's no synchronization, so the outcome is non-deterministic. Go ships a race detector (go test -race, go run -race) that instruments memory accesses and reports both conflicting accesses with stack traces. It's a standard part of Go CI.

.NET parallel: .NET has no built-in single-flag race detector as mature as Go's; you rely on review of lock and Interlocked use or platform tools. That Go's detector is a first-class test flag is worth mentioning as a genuine strength of the toolchain.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between a buffered and an unbuffered channel in Go?
options: Only buffered channels can be closed or used with range.
An unbuffered channel stores an unlimited number of values, while a buffered one can hold only a single value at a time before every send blocks.
Buffered channels are always faster, so unbuffered channels are deprecated.
An unbuffered send waits for a receiver (a rendezvous); a buffered channel accepts up to n values without one, decoupling producer and consumer.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you understand the synchronization implications, not just the syntax.

Model answer: An unbuffered channel (make(chan T)) makes send and receive rendezvous: the sender blocks until a receiver is ready, useful when you need that handoff. A buffered channel (make(chan T, n)) lets sends succeed without a waiting receiver, up to n, useful for decoupling speeds or for results := make(chan Result, len(items)) so goroutines don't block on send.

.NET parallel: Roughly a SemaphoreSlim(0)-style rendezvous versus a bounded BlockingCollection<T> or capacity-bounded Channel<T>: the same coupling-versus-decoupling trade-off.

questions.prompt: How would you limit how many goroutines run concurrently, so you don't open 10,000 HTTP connections?
options: Call runtime.Gosched() in each goroutine to slow them down.
Use a buffered channel of capacity n as a semaphore, or a fixed pool of worker goroutines reading from a shared jobs channel.
Set GOMAXPROCS to the connection limit, because GOMAXPROCS caps the total number of goroutines a Go program may create at any one moment.
Start all 10,000 goroutines and rely on the HTTP client to queue them safely.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: The worker-pool and semaphore pattern, directly relevant to fanning out to many subscribers.

Model answer: Use a buffered channel as a semaphore: sem := make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrent); each goroutine sends into it before working and receives when done, so once it's full further sends block until a slot frees. Alternatively, run a fixed pool of worker goroutines reading from a jobs channel instead of one goroutine per item.

.NET parallel: Identical to wrapping tasks in SemaphoreSlim(maxConcurrent) or using Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between concurrency and parallelism, and what does GOMAXPROCS control?
options: They're synonyms, and GOMAXPROCS sets the maximum number of goroutines a program can create, which defaults to one per CPU core on the machine, so raising it always makes any program faster.
Concurrency structures work as independent pieces; parallelism runs them at the same instant. GOMAXPROCS sets how many OS threads run goroutines simultaneously.
GOMAXPROCS controls the garbage collector's heap size target.
Concurrency requires multiple cores, while parallelism can run on a single core.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Conceptual precision, a classic Rob Pike talking point.

Model answer: Concurrency is about structuring a program as independently progressing pieces (dealing with many things at once); parallelism is executing several at the same instant (doing many things at once). GOMAXPROCS sets how many OS threads run goroutines simultaneously, defaulting to the CPU count. A highly concurrent program can still run on one core by interleaving.

.NET parallel: The same distinction as async/await (concurrency: freeing a thread during I/O) versus Parallel.For or Task.Run across cores (CPU-bound parallelism). If you've explained why async isn't automatically faster, you've reasoned through this.

questions.prompt: How would you version a public API so you can make breaking changes without breaking existing clients?
options: Embed the version only in internal logs, so clients never need to send one.
Prefer additive changes; when a break is unavoidable, version in the URL or a header and run both versions with a communicated deprecation timeline.
Make breaking changes in place and notify clients afterwards, since keeping two versions running in parallel doubles the code and is never worth the effort.
Version every endpoint on every release, even for purely additive changes.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you treat API evolution as an ongoing discipline, not a one-time decision.

Model answer: Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) so most changes need no versioning. When a break is unavoidable, version explicitly, in the path (/v2/orders) or a header, and run both versions in parallel with a communicated deprecation timeline. For event contracts, include a version field in the payload so one topic can carry several versions during a migration.

.NET parallel: ASP.NET Core has first-class support via the Asp.Versioning package; the judgement (additive versus breaking, deprecation windows) is the same. In Go, versioning is usually explicit routing you write yourself.

questions.prompt: A partner team says your API response lacks a field they need. How do you handle it, and prevent it next time?
options: Add the field as required, so every consumer is forced to handle it immediately.
Tell them to parse the data out of a different endpoint's response instead.

Rename an existing field to the name they expect, which is the quickest fix, and then ask every other consumer to update their code to match, since renaming a field is not a breaking change for JSON consumers.
Add the field as an optional, additive change now; prevent repeats with consumer-driven contract tests and a published schema or OpenAPI spec.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Process maturity, not just a technical fix: the JD's self-service tooling and contracts.

Model answer: Immediate fix: add the field as optional and additive so no existing consumer breaks. Systemic fix: consumer-driven contract testing closes this gap; had the team published a contract of what they depend on, the gap could have surfaced in your CI first. Also propose better self-service discovery (a schema registry or published OpenAPI spec).

.NET parallel: Like an internal NuGet contracts library or a gateway with published Swagger docs: the fix isn't just adding the field, it's asking why nobody saw this coming, and the answer is usually better contract visibility.

questions.prompt: What makes an API RESTful, and does the Integration Hub need to be strictly REST?
options: Every endpoint must implement full HATEOAS and the event flow must also be synchronous REST calls, because mixing paradigms breaks consistency.
Resources at URLs, standard verbs, statelessness and meaningful status codes; use REST for subscription CRUD but messaging (Kafka) for the event flow.
An API is RESTful as long as it uses JSON, whatever the URLs and verbs look like.
REST requires server-side sessions so clients don't resend context.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you treat REST as dogma or as one tool among several.

Model answer: Core REST ideas: resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP verbs mapped to actions, statelessness, and meaningful status codes. Most "RESTful" APIs are pragmatic subsets (few implement HATEOAS), which is fine. For the Integration Hub, subscription management is naturally REST-shaped CRUD, but the event flow is better modelled as asynchronous messaging (Kafka) than forced into request/response.

.NET parallel: ASP.NET Web API's controller-per-resource convention nudges toward the same pragmatic subset; the senior half of the question is knowing when not to force something into REST.

questions.prompt: How do you paginate an endpoint that could return millions of rows?
options: Use OFFSET and LIMIT, because the database jumps straight to the requested offset in constant time, however deep the page and however many rows change.
Return all rows in a single response and let the client page through them.
Use keyset (cursor) pagination, WHERE created_at > $last ORDER BY created_at LIMIT n, which stays fast and stable where OFFSET degrades.
Pick rows at random for each page, which avoids hot spots in the index.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Awareness that offset pagination breaks down at scale.

Model answer: OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 gets slower as the offset grows, because the database still scans and discards the skipped rows, and it's unstable when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. Keyset pagination uses the last-seen sort key (WHERE created_at > $last_seen ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20): consistent performance and stable results under concurrent writes.

.NET parallel: The same trade-off EF Core developers hit with .Skip().Take(), which compiles to offset SQL; keyset pagination has to be written by hand in EF too.

questions.prompt: How do you design an API so a partner integration built today doesn't break when you add a required field next year?
options: Add the required field to the current version and reject requests without it, because partners are expected to update within a release cycle, which is how additive contract evolution is meant to work.
Accept any payload without validation, so new fields never break anyone.
Never add a required field to an existing version: new fields are optional with defaults, and anything mandatory ships in a new version with deprecation.
Make every field required from day one, so nothing ever has to change later.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether required fields in a growing contract are understood as a long-term liability.

Model answer: Never add a genuinely required field to an existing contract version: anything new is optional with a sensible default, or ships in a new explicit version old clients never see. If a field must eventually become mandatory, that's a deprecation process (announce, support both, monitor adoption, retire), not a flag flip.

.NET parallel: Like a public NuGet package where you can't add a required constructor parameter without breaking every caller: additive only, or a new major version.

questions.prompt: How would you design a system that normalizes events from 50 partners, each with its own format, into one internal model?
options: Store each partner's raw payload and translate it only when a report is run.
Make all 50 partners send your internal format directly, and push their translation logic into each subscriber service that later consumes the events.
Write one shared parser with a branch per partner inside a single function.
Separate ingestion, a per-partner adapter that translates into a versioned internal model, and the internal routing bus, so one partner can't break the others.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A near restatement of the actual job; expect a version of it in the technical round.

Model answer: Separate ingestion (accept the raw format, minimal validation) from translation (an adapter per partner mapping into your internal versioned event model) from the internal bus that routes normalized events to subscribers. Each adapter is isolated, so one partner's malformed payload or format change can't break the other 49. New partners self-serve: implement the adapter contract, register it, and the platform handles delivery, retries and routing.

.NET parallel: Architecturally an Anti-Corruption Layer, as in translating five shipping carriers' APIs into one IShippingProvider. Say it out loud if you've built something like this in .NET; it's a strong, honest answer even without Go production experience.

questions.prompt: How do you guarantee an event is never lost between your database write and publishing it to Kafka?
options: Use a larger Kafka replication factor, which removes the need for an outbox.
Publish to Kafka first and only then write to the database, because Kafka acknowledges every write durably, so the two systems can never disagree, even if the process crashes between the two calls.
Wrap the database write and the Kafka publish in a try/catch and retry both.
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the change, then publish it by polling or CDC and mark it sent.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you know the transactional outbox by name and reasoning.

Model answer: A database write and a broker publish are two systems with no shared transaction, so a crash between them loses the event. The outbox writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change; a separate poller (or CDC reading the WAL, like Debezium) publishes it afterwards and marks it sent once confirmed.

.NET parallel: MassTransit's AddEntityFrameworkOutbox does this transparently with EF Core. A strong answer: "MassTransit's EF outbox does this automatically; the pattern is the same in any language, and in Go I'd implement it by hand."

questions.prompt: A consumer processes the same Kafka message twice. Is that a bug?
options: No, and consumers can safely ignore duplicates because side effects never repeat.
Yes: Kafka guarantees exactly-once delivery by default, so a duplicate always means the broker is misconfigured and should be fixed on the cluster.
Yes, and the fix is to commit offsets before processing each message.
No: Kafka delivers at least once, so redelivery is expected. The bug would be a consumer that isn't idempotent and double-applies the side effect.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you understand Kafka's actual delivery guarantee.

Model answer: Kafka's default is at-least-once delivery, so redelivery after a crash or rebalance is normal. The bug would be a consumer that isn't idempotent and double-applies the side effect. Fix it at the consumer with an idempotency check, not by forcing Kafka into exactly-once (possible in narrow transactional cases, rarely the simplest answer).

.NET parallel: A property of the messaging system, not the language. Azure Service Bus's PeekLock mode and RabbitMQ have similar at-least-once defaults, so experience there transfers directly.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between choreography and orchestration, and which fits the Integration Hub?
options: Choreography lets services react to events with no coordinator; orchestration has a central engine like Temporal. Use orchestration for the core flow, choreography for fan-out.
Orchestration means every subscriber reacts on its own, while choreography uses a central workflow engine, so Temporal is a choreography tool by design.
Use one central workflow that controls every downstream team's business logic.
They are identical, so the choice only affects naming.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A named architectural distinction directly relevant to how the platform's flows are structured.

Model answer: Choreography: each service reacts to events independently and the flow emerges from local decisions; decoupled, but the end-to-end flow is hard to see. Orchestration: a central coordinator (Temporal) directs each step and tracks progress. For the Integration Hub: orchestration for the platform's own core delivery flow, so failure, retry and replay state is visible, and choreography for fan-out, where each subscriber decides what to do with an event.

.NET parallel: A MassTransit state-machine saga is orchestration; services that just react to messages via consumers are choreography. Name honestly which you've built.

questions.prompt: A partner sends events out of order, with "order shipped" arriving before "order created". How do you handle it?
options: Assume no ordering: buffer briefly and reorder, make state transitions order-tolerant and idempotent, or park events that reference unseen parents and retry.
Process events by arrival time and overwrite state with whatever came last.
Sort all events globally by timestamp before processing any of them.

Reject the partner's integration, since events generated in order are guaranteed to arrive in order across the internet and any deviation is a partner bug, so reordering logic is never needed on your side.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Real-world messiness handling, since partner-controlled contracts rarely behave perfectly.

Model answer: Layered options: buffer and reorder within a short window if delays are small and bounded; make consumers tolerate out-of-order arrival with idempotent, order-independent transitions ("shipped" sets a flag instead of assuming a prior state); or park an event that references a not-yet-seen parent and retry after a delay. The wrong answer is assuming external events arrive in logical order.

.NET parallel: The same problem space as out-of-order messages in Service Bus sessions, or a payment processor's "pending" and "succeeded" webhooks arriving in either order.

questions.prompt: How would you let a new partner test their integration without touching production data?
options: Give the partner read access to a copy of production data, since realistic data matters more than isolation and partners can be trusted with it.
Let partners test directly against production during off-peak hours.
Skip testing and fix contract mismatches once they show up in production.
Provide a sandbox with production's contract but isolated data, synthetic event generators, versioned example payloads and a schema-validation endpoint.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A direct match to the JD's self-service tooling and developer experience.

Model answer: A sandbox environment mirroring production's contract but backed by isolated test data, plus synthetic event generators so a new adapter can be exercised without a live partner. Add clear, versioned example payloads and a validation endpoint that checks outgoing events against the schema before they reach the real pipeline.

.NET parallel: Like Stripe's test mode, or a WireMock test-double server for a .NET team building against a third-party contract.

questions.prompt: Do you need both a dead-letter queue and a circuit breaker?
options: No: retries make both unnecessary as long as they're unlimited.
Yes, but only one may be active at a time.
Yes: a circuit breaker stops calls to a fully down dependency, while a DLQ quarantines individual messages that fail even when the dependency is healthy.
No: a circuit breaker already dead-letters every failing message automatically, so adding a separate dead-letter queue just duplicates the same protection.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you see the two as complementary rather than redundant.

Model answer: They solve different failure shapes. A circuit breaker protects against a fully down dependency by stopping calls for a cooldown, avoiding wasted retries. A dead-letter queue catches individual messages that fail even when the dependency is healthy (a malformed payload, a permanent rejection). Use the breaker to stop hammering a dead endpoint and the DLQ to quarantine messages that fail while it's up.

questions.prompt: How would you implement idempotency for an endpoint that processes payments?
options: Hash the request body and compare it to the last ten requests in memory, silently doing nothing on a match so the client doesn't receive a duplicate response, which also survives restarts and works across instances.
Check whether the key exists after charging the card, then roll back if it does.
Require a client-supplied idempotency key, insert it under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect, and return the stored result on repeats.
Rely on the payment provider to reject duplicates, so no key is needed on your side.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Precision; payments are the canonical example because subtle mistakes are expensive.

Model answer: Require the caller to supply an idempotency key (a UUID per logical attempt). Atomically check-and-insert it into a table with a unique constraint before any side effect, in the same transaction as the side effect. If the key exists, return the stored result of the original attempt rather than reprocessing, and don't silently no-op, because the caller still needs a response.

.NET parallel: Stripe's .NET SDK supports RequestOptions.IdempotencyKey; if you've integrated Stripe you've used this from the client side. Implementing it server-side in Go is the same idea, inverted.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and which suits the Integration Hub?
options: Choose exactly-once delivery, because modern brokers guarantee it end to end across independent systems at no extra cost or added complexity.
Choose at-most-once, since losing an occasional event is simpler than handling duplicates.
At-least-once never produces duplicates, so idempotency isn't required.
At-most-once can lose messages, at-least-once can duplicate them, and exactly-once is effectively at-least-once plus idempotency. Choose at-least-once with idempotent consumers.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Precise definitions plus a defensible choice; answering "exactly-once" without the cost is the trap.

Model answer: At-most-once: zero or one deliveries, so silent loss is possible. At-least-once: one or more, no silent loss but duplicates. Exactly-once: the ideal, but across independent systems it usually means effectively-once via at-least-once plus idempotent consumers. For the Integration Hub: at-least-once with idempotent consumers everywhere; simpler and more robust.

.NET parallel: The same trade-off as Service Bus's PeekLock (at-least-once, explicit completion) versus ReceiveAndDelete (at-most-once).

questions.prompt: How does Temporal achieve durability without explicit checkpoint and recovery code?
options: It records each step in an append-only event history; after a crash a worker replays the workflow, reusing recorded activity results, so the code must be deterministic.

It snapshots the whole worker process memory to disk every few seconds and restores the latest snapshot after a crash, so any code works unchanged, and its activities run outside the workflow history.
It stores the workflow's state in the client application's database tables.
It re-runs every activity from scratch after a crash, so side effects simply repeat.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you understand the event-sourcing mechanism underneath, not just "it works."

Model answer: Temporal records every meaningful step (activity start and completion, timers, signals) in an append-only event history. If the worker crashes, another replays the history against the same workflow code, but replayed activity calls return their recorded results instead of re-executing, so the code arrives back where it crashed and continues. That's why workflow code must be deterministic: no direct randomness or wall-clock reads.

.NET parallel: The same idea as event sourcing (rebuilding state by replaying a log), as with EventStoreDB or Marten; Temporal applies it to orchestration logic rather than domain state.

questions.prompt: What's a compensating transaction, and when do you need one instead of a retry?
options: A compensating transaction is the database rolling back automatically when a later step fails, which works across services because every system shares one log.
It's only needed for read-only operations that never change state.
When a step already succeeded but a later step failed: instead of retrying, run an explicit, business-aware inverse such as sending a cancellation.
It means retrying the failed step until it eventually succeeds.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you distinguish retrying an operation from undoing a completed one.

Model answer: Retrying assumes the operation hasn't succeeded yet. A compensating transaction is needed when an operation did succeed but a later step failed, so the completed step must be deliberately undone (a partner was notified but billing failed, so you send a cancellation rather than re-notifying). Compensations aren't automatic rollbacks; they're inverse actions designed per step, and not everything has a clean inverse.

.NET parallel: If you've built a MassTransit state-machine saga or hand-rolled compensation in an order pipeline, you've designed these; only the orchestration mechanism differs.

questions.prompt: Your idempotency key is a hash of the request body. What could go wrong?
options: Nothing can go wrong, because a cryptographic hash guarantees that two logically identical requests always produce the same key, whatever metadata changes.
Hashing is too slow for idempotency, so keys should be random per request.
Different requests with identical bodies collide, and retries that vary any field (like a timestamp) hash differently and slip through; use a client-supplied key.
A body hash makes retries impossible, because every retry is always rejected.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you've thought through edge cases of key design, not just the existence of a key.

Model answer: Hashing the body dedupes identical retries, but two genuinely different requests with the same body collide, and a client that sends the same logical operation with slightly different metadata (a timestamp) gets a different hash each time, silently defeating deduplication. A client-supplied key representing "this one logical attempt" is more robust.

.NET parallel: This is why Stripe requires the client to generate and send the key explicitly rather than deriving it from the body.

questions.prompt: How would you handle a poison-pill message that crashes your consumer every time?
options: Catch the failure instead of crashing, and cap attempts per message so it moves to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying forever.
Restart the whole consumer group whenever the message is read.
Delete the topic partition that contains the message.
Retry it indefinitely with a short delay, because given enough attempts every message eventually succeeds and dead-lettering hides real bugs.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Recognition of a failure mode that naive retry logic makes worse.

Model answer: Without a cap, a message that crashes the consumer causes a restart, a re-read (it was never acknowledged) and another crash: an infinite loop that can take down the consumer group. Fix it in two parts: catch and log the failure so the consumer keeps processing other messages, and enforce a maximum attempt count, after which the message goes to the DLQ. "Retry forever" is never the right default.

.NET parallel: Azure Service Bus's MaxDeliveryCount dead-letters a message automatically after N failed deliveries: the platform-native version of this pattern.

questions.prompt: Two requests race to update the same order's status. How do you prevent a lost update?
options: Wrapping both updates in transactions is enough, because PostgreSQL's default isolation level serializes all writes to the same row automatically, which also keeps every query fast.
Use a longer database timeout so the second request waits its turn.
Under read committed a plain transaction isn't enough: lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or use optimistic concurrency with a version column.
Cache the order in memory and update the cache instead of the database.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Practical knowledge of database locking, not just "use a transaction."

Model answer: Under Postgres's default read committed, both transactions can read the old value before either commits, and the second write overwrites the first. Fix with row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so the second blocks until the first commits, or optimistic concurrency with a version column (UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, checking rows affected) and a retry on conflict.

.NET parallel: Exactly what EF Core's optimistic concurrency (a RowVersion column and DbUpdateConcurrencyException) is for; in Go with Postgres the version check is just explicit in your SQL.

questions.prompt: How would you design a schema that supports replaying events from an arbitrary point in the past?
options: Store every accepted event durably with type, version, payload, idempotency key and created_at, index the time column, and replay through the same idempotent path.
Store events in Kafka only, with a retention of a few hours.
Replay by re-sending events directly to subscribers, skipping the idempotency check.
Keep only the latest event per entity and rebuild older history from application logs whenever a replay is needed, since logs record every event anyway.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you treat the event log as a durable, queryable source of truth.

Model answer: Store every accepted event durably: an events table with id, type, version, payload, idempotency_key and created_at, indexed on created_at and type. Replay becomes a query (WHERE created_at BETWEEN $1 AND $2) feeding rows back through the same ingestion and routing path, reusing the idempotency check so already-delivered events aren't duplicated downstream.

.NET parallel: Structurally the same as an audit or event-sourcing table in SQL Server with EF: append-only, timestamp-indexed, queried by range.

questions.prompt: When would you use a JSONB column in Postgres instead of a fully normalized schema?
options: Never use JSONB, since Postgres can't store or query JSON at all.
JSONB for variable payloads you rarely filter on; real indexed columns for fields you query, filter or join on, often both in one hybrid table.
Always prefer JSONB, because Postgres indexes every key inside it automatically and it is faster to filter than regular columns for any query shape.
Store the idempotency key and event type inside the JSONB blob only.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Practical schema-design judgement, relevant to storing flexible event payloads.

Model answer: JSONB fits data whose shape varies by event type or version and isn't queried by its internal fields often, such as the payload itself, avoiding an ever-migrating column-per-field schema. Structured columns fit what you query, filter, index or join on and whose shape is stable (idempotency key, type, status, timestamps). The events table is a hybrid: fixed columns plus a JSONB payload.

.NET parallel: EF Core's JSON column mapping exists for exactly this hybrid case.

questions.prompt: How would you add a NOT NULL column to a production Postgres table without downtime?
options: Drop and recreate the table with the new column, then reload the data.
Add the column as NOT NULL with a default in one migration during peak traffic, since running application code never inserts rows while a migration runs.
Add the column as NOT NULL first and backfill it afterwards.
Add it as nullable, deploy code that writes it, backfill in batches, then add the NOT NULL (or a validated CHECK) once no nulls remain.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Operational schema-change discipline, a common senior trap question.

Model answer: Adding NOT NULL in one step can rewrite or validate the whole table under a lock, and the constraint immediately breaks in-flight inserts from code that doesn't supply the field yet. The safe sequence: add the column nullable, deploy code that writes it, backfill existing rows in batches, then add NOT NULL (or a CHECK validated separately) once no nulls remain; each step deployable and reversible.

.NET parallel: The same multi-step discipline as splitting an EF Core migration across deploys: add nullable, backfill, then enforce.

questions.prompt: What's a connection pool, and why does it matter more in Go than you might expect from .NET?
options: Reuse open connections instead of opening one per query; Go's database/sql defaults (unlimited open, 2 idle) usually need explicit tuning.
Setting MaxOpenConns to unlimited is the safest production default.
Go's database/sql opens a new connection per query and has no pool, so you must build one yourself; its defaults cap connections at your CPU count.
Connection pooling only matters for read replicas, never the primary.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Awareness of database/sql's pooling behaviour, which feels less automatic than EF Core's.

Model answer: A pool reuses open connections across requests instead of paying TCP and authentication per query. database/sql manages one, but its defaults (MaxOpenConns unlimited, MaxIdleConns = 2) are often wrong for production; unbounded open connections under load can exceed Postgres's max_connections and fail during spikes. Tune SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns and SetConnMaxLifetime.

.NET parallel: ADO.NET and EF Core pool transparently with saner defaults; in Go the configuration is explicit, worth knowing cold.

questions.prompt: How would you unit test a Go function that calls an external partner API?
options: Depend on a small interface (PartnerClient) and swap in a fake in tests; use httptest.NewServer when you want to exercise the real HTTP client code.
Call the real partner API from unit tests, so the tests prove the integration works.
Replace http.DefaultClient globally inside the test, so that every package in the test binary uses your mock without any changes to the production code.
Skip unit tests for code that does I/O and rely on end-to-end tests.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Whether you reach for interfaces to isolate the network call rather than mocking http.DefaultClient globally.

Model answer: Define a small interface (PartnerClient with Send(Event) error) instead of calling http.Post inline. Production uses a real implementation; tests use a fake that returns canned responses or errors, so retry, error-handling and idempotency logic are tested without the network. httptest.NewServer spins up a real local server for integration-style tests of the HTTP code path.

.NET parallel: Equivalent to injecting IHttpClientFactory or a custom interface and substituting a mock (Moq, NSubstitute); Go uses implicit interfaces instead of a DI container registering the mock.

questions.prompt: Production is dropping events intermittently. How would you debug it?
options: Add more Kafka partitions, which fixes dropped events in most cases.
Trace known-dropped events by correlation id, check dead-letter contents and consumer lag for that window, and only then suspect silent, unlogged loss.
Assume silent data loss in Kafka and open a ticket with the broker vendor.
Restart every consumer and redeploy the latest build first, since intermittent drops are almost always cleared by a restart and need no investigation.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A structured incident-response approach, not just "I'd check the logs."

Model answer: Start with observability: search logs and traces by correlation id for a few dropped events to see which hop they stopped at. Check dead-letter counts and contents for the window: if events are there, the drop is a caught failure with a stored reason. Check consumer lag: rising lag suggests a slow or crashing consumer, not loss. Only then is silent, unlogged loss the working theory.

.NET parallel: The method is identical in .NET with Application Insights: operation_Id instead of a hand-rolled correlation header, same sequence.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes unit, integration and contract tests, and where does each fit in the Integration Hub?
options: Integration tests are only for the front end; back ends need unit tests only.
Unit tests isolate logic, integration tests cover real Postgres and Kafka wiring, and contract tests protect the adapter interface other teams build against.
Unit tests should use the real database so they catch wiring problems.

Contract tests replace integration tests by running the full system end to end against production, so unit tests aren't needed for platform code, since contract tests already exercise the real database and broker.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A structured testing vocabulary, matching the JD's quality mindset.

Model answer: Unit tests exercise one function or type with dependencies mocked (idempotency logic, retry classification). Integration tests exercise real interactions with Postgres and a Kafka broker via Docker, verifying the wiring. Contract tests verify producer and consumer expectations still match without a full environment. Unit tests dominate core logic, integration tests cover infrastructure wiring, contract tests protect the adapter interface.

.NET parallel: xUnit or NUnit unit tests, WebApplicationFactory integration tests and Pact contract tests: the same pyramid with different tooling.

questions.prompt: How would you roll out a risky change to the Integration Hub without risking all partner traffic?
options: Skip monitoring during the rollout so alerts don't distract the team.
Deploy to every instance at once during a quiet hour, since rolling back a full release is faster than managing a gradual rollout across partners.
Canary to a small share of traffic or low-risk partners, gate behaviour behind feature flags, or shadow-launch and compare outputs without using them.
Ask partners to test the change in production for you before launch.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Safe deployment practice, tied to the JD's safe rollout language.

Model answer: A canary (route a small percentage of traffic, or a few low-risk partners, to the new version and watch error rates); feature flags to toggle behaviour without redeploying; or a shadow launch (run new logic alongside old and compare, using only the old result) to validate correctness first. For a new routing algorithm, shadow mode gives real production comparison with zero delivery risk.

.NET parallel: Azure App Service deployment slots with traffic percentages, or Microsoft.FeatureManagement and LaunchDarkly: the same practice with different tooling.

questions.prompt: How do you decide what should page someone at 3am versus just log a warning?
options: Page only when CPU usage crosses a fixed threshold on any host.
Page on every warning and every retried message, because over-alerting is always safer than missing an incident and engineers can mute what they don't need.
Never page at night; collect every problem for the morning stand-up.
Page on user-impacting symptoms that need a human now, such as rising DLQ depth or a partner fully down; log everything else, to avoid alert fatigue.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: On-call and alerting judgement; the JD mentions an on-call rotation they keep uneventful.

Model answer: Page on symptoms that are user- or business-impacting and need a human now: DLQ depth past a threshold, a partner integration fully down, elevated ingestion error rates. Log or notify non-urgently for informative things: a message retried then succeeded, a background job running slow. Alert on symptoms of real or imminent impact, not every internal anomaly; over-alerting causes fatigue, which is itself a reliability risk.

.NET parallel: The same philosophy applies to Application Insights alert rules or Datadog monitors.

questions.prompt: What would you put in a runbook for the Integration Hub's on-call engineer?
options: Just the phone number of the engineer who built the system.
A full architecture history of the platform, so the on-call engineer understands every design decision before taking any action during an incident.
Map each alert to where to look, likely causes and safe first actions, plus how to replay events, check consumer lag and escalate.
Commands to drop and recreate topics, so incidents can be reset quickly.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Operational thinking beyond writing code, including tooling non-engineers can use.

Model answer: Map specific alert conditions to first actions: for "DLQ depth alert for partner X", where to look (a dashboard or query), likely causes (partner outage, bad deploy, schema mismatch) and the safe first response (nothing destructive; check before acting). Document how to replay a batch of events, check consumer lag, and whom to escalate to, so someone unfamiliar with the internals can handle common cases at 3am.

questions.prompt: How should you answer "tell me about a technical decision you made with incomplete information"?
options: Tell a real story where you decided: what was unclear, what you chose and why, what you'd change, and how you validated it afterwards.
Give a hypothetical answer about what you would do, rather than a real story.
Say you avoid decisions until all information is available.
Describe a situation where your manager eventually decided for you, since showing you deferred to authority under uncertainty is the safest answer.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A direct match to the JD's "comfort making decisions with an incomplete picture." They want a real story, not a hypothetical.

How to prepare: Pick a real example where you designed rather than just implemented, such as the NTT Data microservices architecture or the Andritz real-time pipeline. Structure it: what was unclear, what you decided anyway and why, what you'd do differently with more information, and how you validated the decision (metrics, feedback, it held up in production). Avoid a story where someone else resolved the ambiguity for you.

questions.prompt: How do you decide when to use AI-assisted tooling and when rigor matters more?
options: Only use AI to write tests, and never production code.
Never use AI tools, since they can't help with any part of back-end work.
AI helps with boilerplate, scaffolding and exploring unfamiliar APIs; slow down and review closely for money, concurrency, idempotency, security and live migrations.
Use AI-generated code everywhere without extra review, because AI tools are most reliable on exactly the concurrency and security code that's hardest to write.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: A direct match to the JD's "AI-assisted delivery fluency, and clear judgment on where it helps vs. where rigor matters."

Model answer shape: AI tools are strong for boilerplate, first-draft scaffolding and exploring an unfamiliar API quickly, which is genuinely useful when ramping up on Go. Rigor matters more, and AI-generated code needs closer review, for anything touching money, idempotency or concurrency logic, security boundaries (secrets, auth) or live database migrations: exactly this role's domain. A concrete personal example of each lands better than a generic policy.

questions.prompt: How should you answer "tell me about a time you learned a new technology quickly to deliver something"?
options: Claim existing production experience in Go even if you don't have it, because admitting you're still learning the language is always disqualifying.
Explain that you prefer to stay in the technologies you already know.
Use a real example (such as RabbitMQ/InfluxDB or Python/Node) and frame the Go ramp-up as the same proven pattern repeating.
Describe a technology you read about but never actually delivered with.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Directly relevant to your situation, ramping up on Go under time pressure; a chance to tell a true, on-topic story.

How to prepare: Use a real example (RabbitMQ and InfluxDB at Andritz, or picking up Python and Node at Coderoad) and be honest that the Go ramp-up for this role is the same pattern repeating. Framed as "here's my track record of getting productive in a new stack fast", backed by a concrete prior example, it's a plus, not a liability.

questions.prompt: How do you approach code review, both giving and receiving it?
options: Approve quickly without reading, since trust matters more than review.
Only review code from senior engineers, since juniors' code is reviewed by others.
Separate real bugs and security issues from style preferences, suggest concrete alternatives, and review AI-generated code hardest in risky areas.
Treat every comment as a blocking change request regardless of severity, and avoid suggesting alternatives so the author learns to find the fix themselves.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Collaboration style, relevant to a role building tooling and standards other teams will use.

How to prepare: Distinguish comments by severity (a genuine bug or security issue versus a style preference), explain how you give actionable feedback (suggest a concrete alternative, don't just flag a problem), and mention how AI-assisted changes shift your review posture: reviewing AI-generated code for the same risk categories as before, such as concurrency, security and money-handling logic.

questions.prompt: How should you describe a production incident you were involved in?
options: Only mention incidents that took down the whole company.
Cover what broke, how it was detected, the immediate fix, the root cause, and above all what changed afterwards so it can't silently recur.
Say you've never been involved in an incident.
Focus on how quickly you personally fixed it and who caused it, leaving out the follow-up work because postmortems are mostly paperwork that interviewers skip.
questions.explanation:
What they're testing: Real incident experience and whether you drive follow-through (a postmortem, an actual fix) rather than just firefighting.

How to prepare: Structure it as what broke, how it was detected, the immediate fix, the root cause, and, most important, what changed afterwards (a new alert, a new test, a runbook entry) so the same failure can't recur silently. A smaller "caught a bug before it became one" story is fine; the interviewer is gauging your instinct toward systemic fixes, not the size of the fire.

questions.prompt: When asked to "design the Integration Hub", what should you do first?
options: Clarify scope out loud: partner count and peak events/sec, push or pull, latency needs and delivery guarantees, and state your assumptions.
Ask the interviewer to design it first, then critique their design.
Start drawing Kafka, Temporal and the outbox straight away, because asking questions signals uncertainty and wastes the limited time of the interview.
Pick the most scalable architecture possible, regardless of the stated scale.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 of the walkthrough: clarify scope and requirements, always out loud.

Ask how many partners and events per second at peak (assume dozens of partners, low thousands per second), whether partners push webhooks or you poll them (assume inbound webhooks), what latency is acceptable (seconds), and whether exactly-once is a hard requirement (assume at-least-once with idempotent consumers, and say why). Stating assumptions aloud rather than silently picking them is itself part of what's evaluated: it shows you know these are real design decisions, not defaults.

Then draw the pipeline: ingestion API (HMAC verification, per-partner rate limits), schema validation, outbox plus DB in one transaction, Kafka partitioned by a stable key, independent consumer groups per subscribing team, idempotency checks, and a dead-letter table, with correlation ids and secrets management cutting across.

questions.prompt: In the Integration Hub's ingestion path, where does the idempotency check belong relative to the outbox insert?
options: Before the outbox insert and in the same transaction, so a partner's retried webhook is rejected as a duplicate and never reaches the outbox.
Nowhere; partners never retry webhooks, so duplicates can't happen.
In a separate transaction after the outbox insert has committed.
After the event has been published to Kafka, so that every consumer can decide independently whether a partner's retried webhook was really a duplicate.
questions.explanation:
Deep dive from the walkthrough: "How do you handle a partner retry causing a duplicate?"

Check the idempotency key at ingestion before the outbox insert, inside the same transaction, so a duplicate never even reaches the outbox. The outbox row and the business write commit atomically, which is the point where "we accepted this event" becomes durable regardless of whether Kafka is reachable; the background publisher retries until the row is published.

Trade-off worth naming: putting the outbox at the ingestion boundary is simpler than trying to make Kafka transactional with the source database, and doesn't require Kafka transactions spanning services you don't own.

questions.prompt: If the Integration Hub must handle 10x the partners, what is the main bottleneck to watch?
options: The correlation-id middleware, which serializes all requests.
The single Postgres instance behind the outbox: ingestion scales horizontally and consumers scale with partitions, but write volume eventually needs sharding.
The stateless ingestion API, because it can't run more than one instance behind a load balancer and therefore caps the platform's throughput entirely.
Kafka consumer groups, which can never have more than one consumer each.
questions.explanation:
Deep dive from the walkthrough: "How do you scale this to 10x the partners?"

Kafka scales horizontally by adding consumer instances per group, up to the partition count. The ingestion API scales behind a load balancer because it's stateless. The bottleneck to watch is the single Postgres instance backing the outbox: past a certain write volume, sharding or read replicas become a real conversation, worth naming even if you wouldn't build it on day one.

Related trade-offs to say out loud: at-least-once plus idempotent consumers over exactly-once; orchestration (Temporal) for the core pipeline but choreography for subscriber reactions, since one workflow controlling every downstream team would recreate the coupling the platform exists to remove.
